common_name: Hooker's Onion (Hooker Chives, Chinese Mountain Leek)

planting.note: Plant root divisions or nursery starts in spring in rich, consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun; established clumps can also be divided and replanted in early fall in mild-winter climates.

directions: Set divisions with a few inches of intact root mass into loose, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist, and mulch to keep the shallow root zone from drying out. Unlike most alliums, Hooker's onion is grown chiefly for its thick, faintly cumin-scented white roots as well as its flat, grass-like leaves, both of which are eaten fresh, pickled, or stir-fried in the cuisines of the eastern Himalayas and southern China where the plant originates. It spreads steadily into dense clumps in the moist shade or part shade of a woodland-edge bed and is one of the few alliums that genuinely thrives without full sun. Dig and divide congested clumps every year or two in spring, replanting a portion immediately to keep the patch productive and harvesting the rest roots and all.

common_name: Gerald Derouen Louisiana Iris (Vivid Red Award-Winning Louisiana Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in late summer or fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Plant rhizomes shallowly in consistently moist to wet, slightly acidic, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Gerald Derouen is a Louisiana Cajun-bred cultivar prized for its clear, saturated velvety red flowers held on strong, well-branched stalks, and it remains one of the standard reds against which newer red Louisiana iris introductions are still compared. Like other Louisiana iris it performs best where its roots never fully dry out, making it an excellent choice at a pond edge, in a rain garden, or in a naturally low, poorly drained corner of the landscape. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in late summer, replanting fans with a few inches of rhizome promptly since the roots dry out quickly once exposed.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container stock in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade; in zone 9 the soft stems are killed to the ground by hard freezes but the plant regrows readily from the base.

directions: Plant rooted cuttings in well-drained soil in partial shade to filtered sun, where the soft, gray-green, ginger-scented foliage keeps its best color out of the harshest afternoon heat. Misty plume bush is a fast-growing southern African shrub that produces dense, upright plumes of small lavender-pink flowers in winter, when few other tender shrubs are blooming, making it valuable for extending color and pollinator forage into the cool season along the Gulf Coast. It tolerates poor, dry soil once established and needs little supplemental water beyond an occasional deep soak during extended drought. Cut the woody framework back hard in late winter after bloom to renew dense, bushy growth for the following season; in zone 8b the roots survive most winters even when the top is lost to frost.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

common_name: Devil's Trumpet (Hindu Datura, Downy Thorn Apple)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6 weeks before last frost or direct sow once soil has warmed well past 70°F; nick the hard seed coat and soak overnight to speed erratic germination.

directions: WARNING: ALL PARTS OF THIS PLANT ARE HIGHLY TOXIC — leaves, flowers, and especially the spiny seed pods and seeds contain potent tropane alkaloids that can cause severe poisoning if ingested; site away from children and pets and wash hands after handling. Datura metel is an Old World tropical shrub-like annual (perennial where winters stay above roughly 25°F) grown for its large, upward-facing, intensely fragrant trumpet flowers, most often in shades of purple, lavender, or creamy yellow with some cultivars bearing showy double or triple-layered blooms that open at dusk. Plant in full sun in well-drained, only moderately fertile soil, since rich soil produces lush foliage at the expense of flowering; the plant tolerates heat and drought well once established. In zone 9 it often self-sows and returns from seed each year even where the parent plant is killed by winter cold, and deadheading spent pods before they split will reduce this volunteer spread if it is not wanted.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring after frost danger passes in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; in zone 8b–9 the plant is usually killed back to the crown by hard freezes but regrows from the roots once the soil warms.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Ceylon leadwort is a sprawling, semi-scandent subshrub found through the tropics and subtropics of Asia and Africa that bears loose spikes of small white flowers with a slender green calyx, blooming most heavily where it gets some relief from the hottest afternoon sun. It spreads slowly by root suckers to form an informal, arching mound and works well tucked under high tree canopy or along a shaded fence line where fewer flowering shrubs perform. It is drought tolerant once established and needs little care beyond an annual cutback in late winter to control size and encourage fresh flowering growth; wear gloves when handling cut stems, since the sap can irritate sensitive skin.
